metadata.description: Contextual help topics for the Undercroft suite.

topics.title: Layout and Panes
topics.summary: Every tool uses the same three-pane layout: choose on the left, work in the center, see details on the right.
details: Use the buttons at either end of the header to show or hide the left and right panes. Hiding a pane gives the center more room.

The left pane is where you pick or create what you're working on, and where a tool keeps its palettes and settings. The center pane shows the thing itself. The right pane shows details for whatever you've selected.
The tool name in the header opens a menu for jumping to any other tool or back to the Dashboard.
Search, your account menu and the appearance menu sit in the header on every page.

topics.title: Search
topics.summary: The search box in the header finds your saved records and help topics from any tool.
details: Type at least two letters. Results show the record's name, its type and the tool that owns it, and help topics are listed in their own group above them.
Use the arrow keys and Enter, or click, to open a result. A record opens in the tool that edits it; a help topic opens on the documentation page.
Search covers records you own, records shared with you, public records, and anything you've saved only in this browser.
On a narrow window the box collapses to a search icon in the header.

topics.title: Appearance
topics.summary: Switch between light, dark and system themes, and pick a color theme, from the palette button in the header.
details: “System” follows your device's light or dark setting. “Light” and “Dark” stay as you choose them.
The color themes (Undercroft, Flatly, Journal, Spacelab, Superhero, Vapor and Sketchy) change the look of the whole suite and work in light or dark mode.
Your choices are remembered in this browser, so they stay set the next time you visit.

topics.title: Undo and Redo
topics.summary: Undo and redo work the same way in every tool, from the toolbar or the keyboard.
details: Press Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac) to undo and Ctrl+Shift+Z (Cmd+Shift+Z) to redo, or use the Undo and Redo buttons in the toolbar.
Each tool keeps its own history, so undoing in one tool never changes your work in another.
Your history survives a page reload in the same browser tab. It is cleared when you close the tab.

topics.title: Saving: This Browser or Your Account
topics.summary: You can use the generator tools without signing in. Where your work is saved depends on whether you are.
details: Signed out, Save keeps your work in this browser only. It stays there until you clear the browser's site data.
Signed in, Save stores the work on the server as a record you own. You can open it from any device and share it.
Signing in doesn't discard what you saved while signed out. Some tools, such as Loom and the group tools, need an account at a particular tier; see Account Tiers.
Sharing and group features need a record saved to your account first.

topics.title: Relationships
topics.summary: Link a record to any other record — an NPC, Location, Monster, Character or more — with a label you type yourself.
details: Under Relationships, choose a type of record, use the search button to pick the specific one, then type how they're related (“Member of”, “Rival of”, “Variant of”, “Requires”, “Parent of”). A suggestion list appears, but any text works.
Note and Value are optional. Value is handy for something that varies, like a reputation (“Friendly”, “Hostile”, or a number).

The link shows on both records. Link an NPC as “Member of” another NPC and the other NPC's list shows the NPC right back. That is also how a faction works: a record becomes one when other records are related to it.
Switch the view to Graph to see the same links as a web centered on this record. Use the open button on a row to jump to the other record in its own tool, and the trash button to remove a link.
Locations commonly use “Parent of” for containment (a region and its towns) and “Connected to” for a road or tunnel between peers.

topics.title: Notes and Generate Note
topics.summary: Each generated record has an optional note. Write your own, or have Claude draft one from the record.
details: A record is complete without a note. Everything the generator rolled already stands on its own.

Type directly in the Notes box, or choose Generate Note to have Claude write a short note from the record's current values — for an NPC, its rolled identity and personality; for a Monster, its type, role and features; for a Wonder, its properties and features; for a Location, its identity and features.
Generate Note replaces the box with the draft. You can edit it freely, and whatever is in the box when you Save is what is saved.
Generate Note needs an Anthropic API key, which an administrator sets once for the whole server in Loom's Auth tab.

topics.title: Documentation and Favorites
topics.summary: The documentation page explains every tool. Star the topics you use most to keep them close.
details: Any ? badge in a tool opens its topic on the documentation page. The search box in the header finds topics too.
On the documentation page, groups in the left list open and close, and picking a topic opens its group and scrolls to it. The search box above the list narrows it.
Click the star next to a topic to favorite it. Your favorites show at the top of the documentation list, on your Dashboard's left pane, and on your Account page.
Some topics are favorites automatically for a tier: Running a Game, for example, is starred for GMs. Un-star it and it stays gone.

topics.title: Characters, Templates and Views
topics.summary: Workbench has two modes: Character, to use a sheet, and Template, to design the layout a sheet uses.
details: A Template is the layout of a sheet for one System: its sections, fields and rolls. A Character is one person's data shown through a Template.
Switch between Character and Template with the toggle at the top of the center pane. Template mode needs GM tier or higher.

With a character open, the View and Edit button beside the toggle switches between playing the sheet (View) and changing the character (Edit). Creating, saving and deleting characters, and the Character Properties actions, are in Edit.
Pick what to open from the Template or Character list in the left pane.

topics.title: Template Properties
topics.summary: A Template's name, System, version and description.
details: Choose the System the Template is built for. The fields you can bind components to come from that System.
Name and description help you and others tell Templates apart in lists.
Select a component on the canvas and this panel gives way to the Component Inspector.
Layout holds the Template's minimum column width, which controls when grids wrap on a narrow screen; see Fitting a Template on Small Screens.

topics.title: Template Components
topics.summary: Build a sheet by dragging components from the palette onto the canvas.
details: The palette offers Container, Icon, Image, Input, Repeater, Select Group, Text, Toggle and Track. Drag one onto the canvas, then set it up in the Component Inspector.
A new component starts with sensible labels and styling, which you can change in the Inspector.
A Container groups other components and can lay them out as a grid or as tabs. A Repeater shows one row for each item in a list on the character, such as an inventory.
Every change can be undone. Clear canvas in the palette's header removes everything at once.

topics.title: Choosing the Right Component
topics.summary: Which component fits a count, a yes/no, a total, or content that depends on a choice.
details: A count shown as filled dots or boxes, like Stress or Harm, is a Track. A Toggle is for a single named state with a few choices.
A single yes/no checkbox is an Input set to checkbox with one option. It stores the option's label when ticked and nothing when unticked, not a true or false value.
A total or modifier is a Text component whose value is a formula such as =sum(...). It is calculated, not stored.

When some content only applies to one branch of a character, such as a different set of abilities for each sub-type, a Container set to tabs with one tab per branch is usually simpler than filtering one list.

topics.title: Component Inspector
topics.summary: Select a component on the canvas to change what it shows, how it looks and when it appears.
details: The Inspector is in the right pane. Its sections run from identity and the component's own settings through Appearance and Behavior to Advanced; the last three start closed unless they hold a non-default value.

Binding or Text tells the component which value to show from the character, or a fixed piece of text. Source or Options is where a list of choices comes from, on components that offer a choice. See Bindings and Formulas.
Behavior settings such as Visible, Collapsible and Locked can use a formula, so they can change with the character.
Changes appear on the canvas immediately and can be undone.
Containers and Repeaters also have a minimum column width and a Stack rows when narrow switch under Behavior; see Fitting a Template on Small Screens.

topics.title: Fitting a Template on Small Screens
topics.summary: Make a sheet wrap and stack on a phone instead of squeezing or running off the screen.
details: A Template's columns share whatever width the screen has, so a wide layout gets cramped on a phone. Minimum column width tells a grid how narrow a column may get: once its columns would be thinner than that, the cells wrap onto more rows instead.

Set it for the whole Template under Layout in Template Properties, a number in rem (1 rem is about one line of text). A new Template starts at 9, which suits most fields. Leave it blank and no grid ever changes.

Set it on a single Container under Behavior to override the Template's value. Use a smaller number for a row of narrow boxes you want to keep side by side, a larger one for a row of fields with long labels, and 0 to never wrap that Container.

A Repeater with several columns shows as a table. Turn on Stack rows when narrow under Behavior and each row becomes a small card, with the column headings as labels, once the table would be thinner than its columns at the minimum width. Without it, a wide table scrolls sideways inside its own box.
Choose Phone above the canvas to see the Template at a phone's width while you edit, and Desktop to return.

topics.title: Bindings
topics.summary: A binding connects a component to a value on the character, using @ and a path.
details: What you type decides how a field is read. Plain text is shown as written, @path reads a value from the character, and =expression calculates one. There is no switch; just type into the same field.

A path is a dot-separated route into the character's data, such as @abilities.strength.score or @inventory.0.name. It works the same in every field that accepts a binding: an Input, a Track's segments, an Icon, an Image's URL, a Container's heading, and Text.
Inside a Repeater's row template, a path starts from that one row. @name there means this item's own name, not the character's name. That includes a Repeater nested inside another.

Binding and Source are different. Binding or Text pulls a value from the character. Source pulls a list of choices from the System, for an Input's dropdown, radio or checkbox options and a Toggle's states. Don't type a value binding into a Source field.
A path can continue into an array's or object's properties, so @components.length counts the items in a list. A number or text value has no properties, so @dc.length on a plain number shows nothing.

topics.title: Formulas
topics.summary: Start a value with = to calculate it from other values.
details: A formula is a math and logic expression: =@level + 2, =max(@str, @dex), =@hp > 0. Mix in bindings with @, text in quotes, and the functions listed in Formula Functions.

Only letters, digits, whitespace and these symbols are allowed: + - * / ( ) . , @ < > = ! ? & | % : ' " _ [ ]. Anything else, such as semicolons or curly braces, fails with “Formula contains unsupported characters”.
Choose between options with if(condition, whenTrue, whenFalse) or condition ? whenTrue : whenFalse. Both work and both can be nested. Every argument of if() is calculated, even the one not used.
Text needs real quotes: ="Level " + @level joins words and a number. Unbalanced quotes make the formula fail.
Before a formula sees a bound value, an empty or missing one becomes 0 and a number written as text, like "15", becomes a number. So a plain @dc is a reliable check for whether a field has a value.

topics.title: Formula Functions
topics.summary: The functions you can use inside a formula.
details: Numbers: abs, ceil, floor, round, sqrt, pow(base, exponent), mod(dividend, divisor) and clamp(value, min, max).
Several values at once: min, max, avg, sum, and, or. not takes one value.

Text: len(value) counts characters (or items in a list), upper and lower change case, split(value, separator) returns a list, and replace(value, search, replacement) replaces every exact match. Plain + also joins text.
signed(value) shows a number with its sign, so signed(@stats.proficiencyBonus) reads +4. The result is text, so use it for display only.

lookup(table, key) returns the whole matching entry from a System list, so =lookup('abilities','str').color reads that entry's color. lookupField(table, field, value, result) finds the row of a list on the character whose field equals value and returns its result field.
roller("2d6+3", 0) rolls dice and returns the total when the sheet is being used, and logs the roll. In the Template editor's preview it only returns the second value, since there is nothing to roll.

topics.title: Where Bindings and Formulas Work
topics.summary: Most fields take a binding or a formula, with a live preview, but a few are limited.
details: Under each binding or formula field, a line shows what it currently produces, or a red “Formula error” message if it can't be read.

The preview uses the Template's sample data, not a real character, so a field the System doesn't have, or a path that only means something inside a Repeater row, can show nothing there and still work on a real character.
A Repeater's own binding takes only an @path, because it needs a real list to repeat over and a formula can't give one.
A Container's heading, an Icon's glyph and an Image's URL each take a path, a formula or plain text in the one field.
Colors, and the Visible, Collapsible and Locked settings, take the same @path and =formula values.

topics.title: Adding a Character
topics.summary: Start a character as a blank sheet, with the Build Character wizard, or by importing one.
details: In Edit view, choose New Character. Blank Character asks for a name and a Template and gives you an empty sheet. Build Character and Import Character are covered in their own topics.
Your work is kept in this browser as you go. Save stores it on your account so it is yours to open elsewhere and share.
A character is shown through its Template, so the Template you pick decides which System's rules apply.

topics.title: Build Character
topics.summary: A step-by-step wizard that makes a new character the way your System's rules describe.
details: The first step asks for a name and a Template. The steps after it, such as species, class, background, ability scores and equipment, depend on the System.
If the System has no wizard set up, the wizard says so and you can use Blank Character instead. A GM or creator adds the steps to the System in Loom.
Use Back and Next to move between steps. The character is created at the end, and you can keep editing it after that.

topics.title: Import Character
topics.summary: Bring in a character from another service, such as D&D Beyond, by ID or link.
details: Choose what to import, paste its ID or URL, and select Fetch. Then name the character and choose the Template to show it with.
The import choices are set up in Loom's Import tab by a GM. Only mappings marked as characters appear here.
An imported character remembers where it came from. In Edit view, Re-import in Character Properties fetches it again and merges the changes.

topics.title: The Character Sheet
topics.summary: What's on the sheet and in the side panes while a character is open.
details: The center pane shows the sheet through its Template. In View you play it; in Edit you can change values and the character's details.

The left pane holds your session Notes (kept in this browser only, not saved with the character), Relationships and the character's JSON data. The right pane holds Character Properties, the Dice Roller, Group Chat and Now Showing.
Character Properties has Level Up, Add a Class and Re-import. A button that is greyed out explains why when you hover it.
Level Up and Add a Class walk you through the choices your System's rules call for and then apply them.

topics.title: Dice Roller
topics.summary: Roll dice from the sheet with the dice buttons, a typed expression, or the rolls your System defines.
details: The dice buttons come from your System's own dice. Type an expression such as 2d6 + 3 and select Roll, or use a named roll or move button when the System has them.
A line above the roller says where a roll will go. Choose Post to thread to add it to the open chat thread, Broadcast to show it to the table, or Private to keep it to yourself with nothing recorded.
A formula can roll as well, using roller("2d6+3", 0). See Formula Functions.

topics.title: Group Characters and Party Data
topics.summary: Open a group's characters from its share link, and keep party-wide values like a shared inventory.
details: When you arrive through a group's share link, Group characters in the left pane lists the group's unclaimed characters. Sign in and claim one to play it.
A GM can give a group a Party Template in Loom. The group then appears in the character list, and opening it shows that sheet for the whole group with no character needed.
Changes to party data save as you make them; there is no Save button.

topics.title: Loom at a Glance
topics.summary: Loom is where you manage your content: import it, organize it, and define the Systems and groups it belongs to.
details: Import brings in content from other services. Library lists every saved record and lets you edit, assign and share it.
Systems define a game's properties, dice and vocabulary. Features are the building blocks the Crucible and Vault generators draw on. Macros are lists of actions you can run from the Dashboard.
Groups is where a GM runs a group: its characters, sessions and share link. Users, Community and Admin are for administrators; Admin also holds the server's saved credentials.
Loom needs GM tier or higher, and some tabs need more. Each tab shows only what your account is allowed to do.

topics.title: Importing Content
topics.summary: Fetch content from another source, check how it maps onto Undercroft's records, and save it to your Library.
details: Pick a mapping, choose a data source, enter an ID, URL or file, and select Fetch. The raw data and the mapped result appear side by side below.

The Entities section lists what the mapping produced. Save each one, or use Save All, to add them to your Library. A character fetch can be previewed but isn't saved here; use Import Character in Workbench for that.
Some sources accept several files, or a whole folder, at once. Choose which to bring in with Bulk Import and Import Selected.
A GM can edit a mapping by changing its tree and checking the result against pasted sample data.

topics.title: Mapping Settings
topics.summary: A mapping's Description and Data Type decide how it is listed and where players can use it.
details: Description is the friendly name players see when picking an import, instead of the mapping's file name. Leave it empty and the mapping's ID is shown.
Data Type “Character” means the mapping produces a whole character. It appears in Workbench's Import Character list, so any signed-in player can import their own character without opening Loom.
“Other” is for everything else: backgrounds, classes, species, subclasses, monsters, and mappings that save through this tab.
Data Type only sorts the mapping into the right list; it doesn't change how the data is fetched or mapped.

topics.title: D&D Beyond ID or URL
topics.summary: Enter a character number or sheet URL to fetch a character, or a class, background or species page to fetch that content.
details: A plain number, or a character sheet URL, fetches the live character from D&D Beyond.
A page URL for a class, background or species, such as https://www.dndbeyond.com/classes/2190875-barbarian, fetches that content.
A character is always fetched fresh and is never stored in the Library, because it changes on D&D Beyond. Gated pages need a current D&D Beyond session; see the Admin tab.

topics.title: D&D Beyond Monster ID or URL
topics.summary: Enter a monster number or monster-service URL to fetch that monster's stat block.
details: A plain number, or a URL like https://monster-service.dndbeyond.com/v1/Monster/16909, fetches the stat block.
SRD monsters need no login. Other monsters can be fetched when the server has a current D&D Beyond session saved in the Admin tab and your account has access to them.

topics.title: 5e API Endpoint or URL
topics.summary: Enter an endpoint path or full URL from the 5e SRD API to fetch it.
details: A path such as /api/2024/classes/barbarian, or a full URL, fetches that entry.
A list endpoint such as /api/2024/classes fetches every item it links to, in full, as one batch.

topics.title: Fantasy Statblocks File
topics.summary: Upload a creature note exported from Obsidian's Fantasy Statblocks plugin.
details: The monster is read from the note's statblock block. Everything else in the file is ignored, except a trailing “Description” or “References” section, which becomes the monster's Notes.
Spellcasting is plain text in this format, so spell names and frequencies come through as written and aren't linked to spell records.
Pick several files, or a folder of them, to import a batch.

topics.title: Markdown Item or Spell File
topics.summary: Upload an Obsidian note for a magic item or spell and Loom turns it into a Wonder.
details: Use the markdown-item or markdown-spell mapping, whichever matches your files. A tag line, an italic type or rarity line and bold field labels fill in the Wonder's fields.
The file's name becomes the Wonder's name, since these notes don't state one inside.
The rest of the text is scanned for known Features, the same way a Wonder imported from the SRD is.
A note with no type or rarity line, such as a lore item, still imports; it just has no rarity, attunement or charges.

topics.title: Node Palette
topics.summary: Build a mapping's tree by adding nodes to whatever is selected.
details: Select a node in the tree, then choose a palette entry to add it. Object and With nodes take fields as children; a Pipeline node takes steps.
Once a Pipeline is selected, the Pipeline Steps list appears: Map, Filter, Flatten, Group By, Sort, Dedup and Custom.

topics.title: Library
topics.summary: Browse, edit and assign every saved record, whatever its type.
details: Choose a Type and then an Item in the left pane. The same choice fills the editor in the center and the details and Share button in the right pane.
This is the one place to reopen and change records you saved from an import. The Entities section on the Import tab only shows the current import's fresh output.
Assigned Systems decides which Systems can see a record. A record assigned to none isn't attached to any System yet.
A new record type is just another record: choose “Kind” as the Type and fill in its ID, label, plural and icon the way you would for a Species.

topics.title: Library Contents
topics.summary: Every saved record from every owner, with its details and Share in the right pane.
details: Unlike the Owned content list on your Account page, which shows only your own records, this covers the whole Library.
Use the Type filter to narrow the list to one kind at a time.
Pick an item to see its owner, created date and last accessed date, and a Share button.
Share opens the same dialog used across the suite: a public link, or view or edit access for a specific user or Group.

topics.title: Assigned Template
topics.summary: Choose which Workbench Template a Character record opens with.
details: Only Character records with a Template assigned show up in Workbench. This is also how an imported character becomes usable there.
The list is limited to Templates built for one of the record's Assigned Systems, so choose a System first if it looks empty.
Assigning a Template doesn't change the character's data. If the Template's bindings don't match the data, parts of the sheet will be empty.

topics.title: Systems
topics.summary: A System is a set of properties plus the records assigned to it, describing one game's rules and vocabulary.
details: Workbench Templates and Characters, and the generators, read their fields, dice and options from a System.
Saving a System needs Creator tier or higher. Use New, Save, Duplicate and Delete in the toolbar; Duplicate copies a System, including a built-in one, under a new ID.
Assign records to a System from the Library tab, using each record's Assigned Systems list, not from here.
If a built-in System is temporarily unavailable, a status message says so and everything else keeps working.

topics.title: System Properties
topics.summary: Each property is one field a Template can bind to, such as Hit Points or Alignment.
details: The asterisk button marks a property Required, and the trash button removes it. Default is used when a new record is created. Minimum and Maximum apply to Number properties.
An Object property holds sub-fields, like an Abilities object with Strength, Dexterity and so on.

An Array property is either an Enum, a fixed list of values shared by every record (such as Rarity), or Records, a repeating group of sub-fields where each record has its own items (such as an Inventory of Name, Quantity and Weight), with a Display field naming what represents each row.
Each value of an Enum has an options row that shows only the columns it needs; see Array Value Options.
Extra properties (JSON) on a value holds anything without its own column, and is kept as you wrote it.
The list a System uses for Forge's NPC types is read most common first: the first entry comes up most often and the last least often, however long the list is.
Preview Data is sample data used when previewing bindings in the Template editor. It isn't part of any real character.

topics.title: System Dice
topics.summary: Give a System its own physical dice, such as Hope and Fear dice or labeled d6s.
details: Add an Array property with the key “dice”. Each value's Name is the die's ID, which is what dice expressions use, for example “2 hopeDie”.
In the value's Extra properties (JSON), set sides to a number, or “F” for a Fate die. You can also add faceMap, to show a label for certain results (a d6 reading “1-3”, “4-5”, “6”), and color.
A System with no “dice” property rolls the standard seven: d4, d6, d8, d10, d12, d20 and d100.

topics.title: Special Property Names
topics.summary: A few property keys are read by other tools, so they appear in their own list.
details: A property moves to the Reserved Keys list as soon as its key matches one of these names; there is nothing to switch on: buildSteps, levelUpBindings, derivedFormulas, fieldRoles, dice, rolls, decks, currency, inventory, travelMeans, levels and casterTypes.
They drive things like Workbench's Build Character wizard, level-up, calculated values, dice and Rolls, card decks, currency, overland travel and encounter difficulty.
fieldRoles tells other tools which of your properties plays which role, such as ability scores or creature type.
Reserved Key Diagnostics, below the Property Inspector, checks each one's shape and flags anything wrong.

topics.title: Array Value Options
topics.summary: The extra columns you can turn on for the values of an Array property, and what each does.
details: Description: rules or flavor text shown under the value's name wherever the options appear, such as a dropdown or checkbox list.
Short name: an abbreviation used where the full name doesn't fit, such as STR for Strength or V, S, M for spell components.
Source ID: a number used to match this value to a code in imported data, such as a D&D Beyond alignment or condition ID. Most hand-written values can leave it blank.
Library kind and Library field: point a value at a kind of record and a specific record or field in it, for example the class a list entry stands for. Picking a record fills in its ID for you.
Record field and Target path: a path into the character a value reads and writes (Record field), or only writes to (Target path), such as stats.hitPoints.current.
Source field: the key of another field in this System whose values are the options for this one, such as a Conditions list for a Tags value.
Binding: which role a value plays for combat tracking. See Combat Bindings.

Cost: a number each value spends from the generation budget, or refunds if negative. It is for properties like Activation and Item Form. If the property is the Vault budget ceiling, this value sets the budget instead.
Weight: how much one unit weighs, for the Dashboard's Inventory Weight calculator. Leave it empty for anything it doesn't total, such as most items.
Anything else about a value goes in its Extra properties (JSON).

topics.title: Combat Bindings
topics.summary: Tell the Combat Tracker and the character sheet which values make up live combat state.
details: Combat Bindings aren't a separate property type. They are whichever Array property has values using a Binding: Resource, Value, Tags or Modifier.

Resource is a number with a maximum, and optional temporary points that absorb damage first, such as Hit Points. Value is a single number, such as Armor Class. Tags is a status list that draws its options from another field, such as Conditions. Modifier is a number that feeds a die roll, such as an initiative bonus.
Each value names its Binding and a Record field, the path into the character it reads and writes. Add as many or as few as your game needs, with any names.
A Resource that needs more than one path, such as a maximum, gets them in the value's Extra properties.
A System with no Binding values simply shows no live combat state.

topics.title: System JSON Preview
topics.summary: A live, read-only view of the System exactly as it will be saved.
details: It updates as you edit above, so you can check what a Save will store.
To change anything, use the fields above; this panel only shows the result.

topics.title: Features
topics.summary: Edit the building blocks that Crucible and Vault assemble monsters and wonders from.
details: Choose a Feature to edit its description, mechanics, categories, the recipe slots, roles and creature types it fits, and the Features it works well with or conflicts with. Comparing near-duplicates, such as several “Dagger” Features, is easy by switching between them.
A brand new Feature starts on the Library tab, where you give it an ID. Everything else is editable here.
Cost Budget is a rough points value, usually 1 to 6. Crucible adds up a monster's Feature costs against its Combat Scaling level's budget.

Scope “Generic” means any monster can use it, which is right for nearly every Feature. “Unique” keeps it out of Crucible's automatic generation, so only mark one Unique when it truly can't be reduced to shared parts.
A note under Scope appears when a Feature has no recipe slots yet. Crucible's automatic generation only fills slots, so an untagged Feature won't be picked.
Suggest Cost & Tags asks Claude for a starting guess at behaviors, recipe slots, roles, creature types and cost. It never saves on its own; review it, then save.

topics.title: Mechanics Type and Notes
topics.summary: What kind of ability a Feature is, and how it works.
details: Type isn't shown in generated output. It decides which editing controls Crucible and Vault offer once the Feature is attached: Weapon Attack and Save Effect get an attack bonus or save DC editor, Active gets a parameters grid, and the other types add nothing extra.
Passive is by far the most common: something that is always true. Use Active only when a value really differs per record, like a scaling number.
Notes is for describing the mechanic in enough detail to write or check a stat block. The Description is what a GM reads. Many passives don't need Notes.
A wrong Type corrupts nothing, but you will get the wrong controls wherever the Feature is used, so match it to what the Feature does.

topics.title: Macros
topics.summary: A Macro is an ordered list of actions you can run with one click from the Dashboard or a journal note.
details: Pick a Macro in the left pane, or create one. Saving a Macro needs Creator tier or higher, and you can share it like any record.
Each action targets one kind of widget, such as WLED, Home Assistant, Soundboard, Handout or Combat. The fields change to match what that type needs.
To run a Macro, add it as a card on a Board widget on your Dashboard. See Board.
The Library tab can also open a Macro as raw JSON.

topics.title: Macro Actions and Timing
topics.summary: Actions run from top to bottom, and you can pause between them.
details: Order matters: dim the lights, then play the sting. Use the up and down arrows on a row, or drag its grip handle, to reorder.
A Timing action named Wait pauses the Macro for that many seconds before the next action. “Play an effect, wait 5 seconds, turn it off” is three actions in a row.
A Macro only keeps running while the page that started it stays open.

topics.title: WLED Lighting Actions
topics.summary: Set a light strip's effect, palette and colors from a Macro.
details: A WLED action's device is chosen from the lighting devices saved in your Dashboard's Lighting widget. The Macro stores the device's alias, never its IP address, so when someone else runs it they map it to one of their own devices the first time. A device with no alias yet is given one.

“Set effect / palette / color” sets a segment's effect, palette, brightness and up to three colors. Effect, palette and brightness can be left unchanged. A cleared color (✕) means off, so every color is applied exactly as the swatches show.

Picking an effect shows its own controls with default values filled in, and dims the colors or palette it doesn't use. The preset, effect, palette and segment lists come from the device itself, so your browser must be able to reach it; if it can't, the saved value is kept.

By default the action turns the light on and turns the device's other segments off, as an instant cut. Untick “Turn the light on if it's off” to stage a look and reveal it later with a Turn on action. Untick “Turn the device's other segments off” when several segments should show at once.
An action can name a segment (for example “North”) instead of a number, which keeps working if segments are renumbered.

topics.title: Home Assistant Actions
topics.summary: Control a Home Assistant light or other device from a Macro.
details: A Home Assistant action targets an entity chosen from a dropdown of your live entities. There is no alias step.
The first time you use one, you are asked to connect your own Home Assistant, with its URL and an access token. It is remembered after that.

topics.title: Group Properties
topics.summary: Named values that belong to the whole group, such as a party inventory.
details: Add a property with the Add Property button in the toolbar, then edit it in the Group Properties pane or in the Properties list.
Mark a property Public to let players change its value, for example to add to the party inventory. Properties that aren't public can only be changed by you.

topics.title: Group System
topics.summary: The System this group runs. Its dice and vocabulary become the default for everyone playing in it.
details: Once set, the System's own dice take priority over each character's own System for quick dice buttons and rolls made in this group. See System Dice.
The list of characters you can add to the group shows only characters assigned to this System. Leave the System blank to allow any character.
With no System set, each character uses its own first System, and a character with none uses the standard seven dice.

topics.title: Group Setting
topics.summary: The Setting the group takes place in, used as the default for Setting-specific data.
details: Optional. Leave it blank for a homebrew or generic game.
Widgets that read Setting-specific data, such as the Calculator's travel means, use it unless that widget is set to something else.

topics.title: Party Template
topics.summary: The Workbench Template that shows the group's party data, with no character needed.
details: The list shows Templates built for the group's System, so set the System first. Leave the System blank to see every Template.
Bind the Template's components only to @group paths, such as a Repeater on @group.inventory. It is shown with no character loaded, so any other binding comes out empty.
Once set, the group appears under Groups in Workbench's character list. Opening it shows this Template with Edit ready, and changes save as you make them.

topics.title: Group Members
topics.summary: Choose which characters are in a group, and which one each player is currently playing.
details: Select a group to see its character list. Tick a character to add it and untick it to remove it. Changes save automatically.

Each character in the group has an Active switch. A player has one active character per group, the one they are playing now; turning one on turns their other off. Players can also switch their own from a session invitation in their Inbox.
Only players with an active character are invited to the group's sessions.

topics.title: Sessions
topics.summary: Schedule your table's real-world game sessions, one-off or repeating, and see who is coming.
details: A session is a live game, with a start time and length, or a play-by-post window, with a range of dates. Times are saved as exact moments and shown to everyone in their own time zone.

A repeating session creates each date on its own as it comes within “Announce this many days ahead”, even if you never open Loom. Repeats keep a fixed spacing, so where clocks change for daylight saving a repeating game's local time can shift by an hour; edit that one date to correct it.
Click a date to edit or cancel just that one, or switch to Whole series. Changing a date's start clears its RSVPs and sends everyone a fresh notice; other edits keep the RSVPs.

Players are invited through their active character, so manage who is active in the group's character list. Setting a player's answer yourself under Attendees ignores the RSVP cutoff and the player maximum.
The reminder is sent that many hours before a live game starts, or before a play-by-post window closes. If the RSVP cutoff passes with fewer players accepted than your minimum, you get an alert.
When a session has a player maximum, extra players can join a waitlist. If someone drops out, the longest-waiting player is accepted and told in their Inbox.
After a session, note which in-world dates it covered and link its chat thread or a Repository recap page. The History view then works as your session log.
Lock posting limits the linked threads to the session window for everyone except you.
Delete session removes a session and all its dates for good. End series stops new dates and keeps the history.

topics.title: Users
topics.summary: Administrators can create accounts and change a user's email, tier and status.
details: Filter by tier, choose a user, and edit their email, tier or status. To add someone, start a new user and give a username, email and password.
You can't change your own tier or status here, so an administrator can't lock themselves out.
Tiers run from Free through Player, GM and Creator to Admin. See Account Tiers.
Each account shows the invite it joined with, if any. See Invites.

topics.title: Invites
topics.summary: A shareable sign-up link that can start new accounts at a chosen tier and shows where each sign-up came from.
details: Use + to create an invite, or select one in the list to edit it in the right pane. An invite has a label (for example where you'll post the link), the tier an account starts at, an optional limit on how many accounts can use it, and an optional expiry. Copy its link and share it. Opening the link brings up the sign-up form with the code filled in.
The starting tier applies only to accounts created through that invite, and an invite can never create an administrator. A high-tier invite is powerful, so keep its limit low or its expiry short.
Each invite lists how many accounts have used it and who they are. A sign-up that is still waiting for its email code counts toward the limit.
Switch an invite off to stop it working without deleting it, or delete it to remove it. Accounts that already joined keep working either way, and changing an invite's tier doesn't change them.
By default an invite code is optional on the sign-up form. The server can instead require one for every new account; that is a setting in the server's configuration file.

topics.title: Systems People Name
topics.summary: The game systems people typed by hand, so you can see which ones are worth adding to the Library.
details: Players can type a system on their profile, and a Recruitment listing can name one. A name that matches a Library System is added as that System; any other name shows up here with how many people used it, never who.
A person counts once per name, however many profiles and listings they used it on. Spellings that differ only in capitals or punctuation are grouped as one name.

This never creates a System. To cover a name that keeps coming up, create the System in the Systems tab first. Its row then shows In the Library, and its button reads Convert: pressing it moves everyone's entries onto that System and the row goes away.
To tidy up before then, change the name in a row and press Rename. If the new name is one already listed, the button reads Merge and the two become one.
The Another system boxes suggest a name once two or more people have used it, so spellings settle on one over time.

topics.title: Admin Overview
topics.summary: An administrator's dashboard for the health of the whole server's content, with the server's saved credentials at the bottom.
details: System Content Health checks every System for problems. Library Content Inventory counts every record by type and flags orphans. Users & Tiers and Groups summarize accounts and groups.
The sections are collapsed until they have something to show. Below them are the D&D Beyond session and Anthropic API key, which have their own help topics.
Each section shows a count and links to the tab that has the details. Select Check now on a section, or Check all, to run it again.
This tab is for administrators.

topics.title: D&D Beyond Session Cookie
topics.summary: The sign-in cookie the server uses to fetch gated D&D Beyond pages. It expires and needs a fresh one now and then.
details: To get a fresh cookie, sign in to dndbeyond.com and open your browser's developer tools (F12, or Ctrl+Shift+I; Cmd+Option+I on a Mac).
Open the Application tab (Chrome or Edge) or the Storage tab (Firefox), expand Cookies in the left sidebar, and select https://www.dndbeyond.com.
Find the row named CobaltSession and double-click directly into its Value cell to select just that text. Copying the whole row grabs every column at once and silently fails.
Paste just that value into the field and click Save. The CobaltSession= prefix is added if you leave it off.
Check now tests the saved cookie against a real D&D Beyond page. The same check runs once a day and whenever the cookie is used for a real fetch.

An expired cookie doesn't show an error. D&D Beyond quietly serves its signed-out preview, which can look like a successful import that is missing content. If an import seems to stop partway, or comes back truncated or empty, check here first.
Treat the value like a password: anyone with it can act as that D&D Beyond account. It expires periodically.

topics.title: Anthropic API Key
topics.summary: The key behind every tool's Generate Note, shared by the whole server.
details: Paste a key from your Anthropic Console account. It is stored encrypted, like any other server credential.
Unlike the D&D Beyond session, an API key doesn't quietly expire, so there is no regular check. “Configured” just means a key is saved.

topics.title: Dashboard Basics
topics.summary: Your landing page: build a play space out of widgets and arrange them how you like.
details: Choose Edit layout to add or remove widgets and to drag a widget by its header to reorder it.
Your layout saves in this browser right away, and syncs to your account once you're signed in, so it follows you to other devices.
The tool menu in the header jumps to any other tool. It doesn't list the Dashboard, since you're already here.
The left pane lists your favorite documentation topics, and a widget's own settings sit in the right pane.

topics.title: Second Screen
topics.summary: Set the resolution, zoom and position of the mirror window for a second monitor or TV.
details: Pick a common resolution, or choose Custom to enter any width and height your second display needs.

Zoom scales everything the mirror shows, for a high-resolution display that draws the same page smaller than you want. You can change it at any time, even while the window is open, and it updates within a few seconds.
In a Chromium-based browser, once you grant permission, the mirror window opens on your second monitor automatically. Elsewhere, drag it onto your second monitor once and it reopens there.
These settings are saved in this browser only, because a monitor arrangement belongs to one computer.

topics.title: Combat Tracker
topics.summary: Run initiative, hit points and conditions for an encounter. Everyone in the group sees a live, read-only copy.
details: Add combatants by searching for a character, NPC or monster, or typing a name. Use Roll initiative (non-characters) to roll for everyone who isn't a player character in one go.
Start combat, then Advance turn to move through the order. Type a number into ±HP to adjust a combatant's hit points, and add or remove conditions from the System's own list.
Show to table makes the encounter visible to the group, and Hide from table takes it away again. The tracker can light each player's seat on their turn; see Table Lighting.
Which values count as hit points, armor class and conditions comes from the System's Combat Bindings.

topics.title: Character Widget
topics.summary: Your own character's vitals at a glance, kept in step with the sheet and the Combat Tracker.
details: Pick one of your characters to see the values its System tracks in combat, such as hit points, armor class and conditions.
Adjust HP or AC and add or remove conditions right here. The change is the same one you would make in Workbench or the Combat Tracker, because they all use the same character record.
Initiative is rolled and sent to the active encounter; it isn't stored on the character.

topics.title: Dice Roller Widget
topics.summary: Roll an expression, your System's named rolls, or a dice pool, and choose where the result goes.
details: Type an expression such as 2d6 + 3, or use the quick dice buttons. A System's named Rolls and Moves and symbol-dice pools appear here when it defines them.
Post to thread records the roll in the open chat thread, Broadcast shows it to the table, and Private shows it only to you with nothing recorded. A line above the roller says where a roll will land.
A rollable table from a journal page can be picked below the expression box.

topics.title: Deck Widget
topics.summary: Draw from a standard playing deck, a tarot deck, or any deck your System adds.
details: Standard playing cards and a tarot deck are always available. A System can add its own decks, such as a harrow deck, and they are listed first. A System that defines a deck with the same name as a standard one replaces it.
Like dice, a draw can be posted to the open thread, broadcast to the table, or kept private.
Cards can carry their own details, such as a suit and rank, as the System defines them.

topics.title: Calculator Widget
topics.summary: Quick tools for a GM: dice odds, travel time, item prices, carried weight and encounter difficulty.
details: Choose a type from the menu: Dice Probability, Travel Time, Item Price, Inventory Weight, or Encounter Difficulty & XP.

Dice Probability shows the average and range of an expression like 3d6. Travel Time uses the travel means your System or Setting defines, with hours per day and a pace; a daily roll or table can run once for each day of the trip.
Item Price prices a saved Wonder. Inventory Weight totals a character's gear, with currency weight optional. Encounter Difficulty & XP reads the System's table of level thresholds.
Travel means and level tables belong to the System and Setting, so the options you see depend on the group.

topics.title: Shop Widget
topics.summary: Let players buy and sell from a Location's shop, live.
details: Choose the Location whose shop the widget shows. A GM opens and closes the shop and manages its money.
Players buy from and sell to an open shop.
A GM can buy or sell on behalf of a player who isn't there, using the “Buying for” and “Selling as” choices.

topics.title: Map Widget
topics.summary: Show a saved map the way the table sees it, with tools to ping, measure and draw.
details: Pick a map to display. Fog of war, walls and doors are shown the way a player sees them.
Ping the map to point something out, Measure distance between two points, Draw an area-of-effect shape, or Draw on the map and choose the color and opacity.
Players can drag a marker for a character they own and open doors that aren't locked. Click a marker with contents to claim an item.
A map's owner can edit any marker from here. Use Orrery to build the map itself.

topics.title: Clock Widget
topics.summary: A segmented progress or countdown clock, like the ones in Blades in the Dark.
details: Give the clock a name and a number of segments, then advance or retreat it, or set the filled segments directly. It can tick forward on its own.
Add the widget again for another clock.
Show to table puts the clock in front of the group, and Hide from table removes it.

topics.title: Calendar Widget
topics.summary: Track the in-world date, and optionally the time of day, for the whole group.
details: The date is read against a Setting's calendar, so the Setting needs a calendar defined in Sanctum. See Calendar.
Every Calendar widget in the group shows the same date. Advance it from one and the others update.
Use Advance or retreat to move by days or minutes. Turn on Track time of day to add a clock, and Auto to let time pass on its own.
Show to table puts the date in front of the group.

topics.title: Lighting Widget
topics.summary: Control a WLED light strip, or a Home Assistant light, from the Dashboard.
details: Add a WLED device with its address (an IP address, host name or full web address), an alias and an optional label. The alias is the device's identity: Macros, Table Lighting and every Lighting card refer to it by alias, never by address, so an address can change without breaking anything.

You can also give a fallback address. Undercroft tries the main address first and uses the fallback when it doesn't answer, for example an IP address at home and an https address through a tunnel when you're away. It returns to the main address when that answers again, and the card says when the fallback is in use.

Use the pencil button to change a saved device's address, fallback, alias or label. Renaming the alias moves your Lighting cards and Table Lighting to the new name, but Macros that use the old alias need the new one.

When Undercroft is opened over https, a browser only lets it reach a lighting device over https as well, and a WLED strip doesn't offer https itself. Setting that up is up to you. A secure tunnel such as Tailscale, or a reverse proxy in front of the device such as Caddy or nginx, both work; Undercroft can't provide one. On a home network you can instead open Undercroft over http and use the device's IP address directly.

A WLED strip shows the segments you've set up in WLED itself. WLED forgets them when it restarts, so use the bookmark button to remember the current segments: their LED ranges, grouping, spacing, reverse or mirror, and blend mode, but not colors or effects.
If the segments later differ from what's remembered, a Restore button appears. It never changes your segments on its own.
Changes made from a Macro, the Combat Tracker or another tab refresh the widget to match.

topics.title: Table Lighting
topics.summary: Light a seat on a lighting strip around the table for whoever's turn it is, and optionally whoever is on deck.
details: Click the lightbulb in the Combat Tracker's toolbar, pick a lighting device you've added in the Lighting widget, and tick “Light the table by turn”.

Choose a segment for the GM, used for every monster, NPC and other non-player combatant, and one for each player. The segment names come from your device, as remembered with “Remember layout” in the Lighting widget. Seats follow the character, so you set them once and they carry into every encounter.

Each segment starts as the Solid effect in green for a player and red for the GM. Open a row's arrow to change its effect, palette, colors or brightness, with the same options as a Macro's “Set effect / palette / color” action.

Tick “Light whoever is on deck” to also light the next combatant. Each segment then has an “On deck” look beside its “Their turn” look. It starts as a copy of the turn look at 10% brightness and follows it until you change it.
On a hidden combatant's turn, or for a player with no segment, the whole table goes dark. Ending combat switches the table's segments off. Only segments you assign here are ever switched off.
The lights follow turns only while this Dashboard stays open in a browser that can reach the device. Reopening the page doesn't change the lights until the turn next changes.

topics.title: Soundboard Widget
topics.summary: Play music and sound effects from links, with a clip library shared by every GM.
details: A clip is a link to audio, with a name and a type: Music loops by default and a sound effect (SFX) plays once. Loop is a setting you can change for yourself afterward.
Add a clip with “Add clip to the shared library”, or search the library to find one. GMs and above can add clips, and everyone's Soundboard can use them. Deleting a clip removes it for everyone.
One music clip plays at a time, and starting another replaces it. Effects play on top of music.
A Macro can play or stop a clip.

topics.title: Board
topics.summary: A private board of reference cards and one-click Macro buttons, arranged in columns.
details: Add a column with Add bucket, and cards with “Add a card”. Start typing a page, Macro, NPC or other saved record to pick it, or paste a link or notes. Pick an icon and color for a card with its pencil.
A card whose whole text is a Macro becomes a big one-click button that runs it. A Macro mentioned inside longer text becomes a small inline chip.
Macros themselves are built in Loom's Macros tab. While you are editing the Dashboard layout, clicking a Macro button opens that Macro in Loom instead of running it.
A Board is private to you and never shown on the second screen. Add the widget again for more boards.

topics.title: Browser Widget
topics.summary: Show a web page or image, to yourself or to the table.
details: Paste a link, or a local file path. A direct image link shows as a picture; anything else loads as an embedded page.
Some sites refuse to be embedded. Use “Open in new tab” when a page doesn't show.
Show to table sends the link to the group.

topics.title: Audio Recorder
topics.summary: Record a whole session's audio in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.
details: Choose New Recording to start, and Stop to finish. Recording is split into chunks of a few minutes, each a standalone audio file you can download. Download all chunks saves them together.
To get a transcript, add a transcription server in Recording Settings and choose it. Without one, you get audio only.
Download transcript saves the text. Download combined session record interleaves the transcript with the Group Chat. A stitch script is offered to join the chunks into one file.
Only the GM sees this widget. The recording stays on your computer.

topics.title: Printing with Press
topics.summary: Pick a source, a template, a size and an orientation, then print a card, chip or sheet.
details: In Selections, choose a Source and give it what it needs (an ID, a file or a record). Then choose a Template, a Format and an Orientation, and select Generate Print to load the data into the preview.
The center pane shows the page. Use Show Back Side to flip between the front and back, Zoom to get a closer look, and Print when it looks right.
Switch between Live Preview of the whole page and Grid View of a single card. Editing in Grid View lets you make changes that apply to that card alone.

topics.title: Selections
topics.summary: The Source, Template, Format and Orientation choices for what you are printing.
details: Selections sit at the top of the left pane. They fold away once a Template is chosen, which opens the Palette beneath them. Open them again whenever you want to change something.
Source decides where the data comes from; the box under it asks for an ID, URL, file or record to match. Only the Templates that support that Source are offered.
After changing the Source or its value, select Generate Print to reload the preview.

topics.title: D&D Beyond Source
topics.summary: Print a D&D Beyond character, class, background or species by URL or ID.
details: Paste a character's ID or URL, or the URL of a class, background or species page such as https://www.dndbeyond.com/classes/2190875-barbarian.
Official and homebrew content both work. A character shared with a link is easiest, because it avoids permission problems.
Select Generate Print to fetch it and load it into the chosen Template.

topics.title: 5e API (SRD) Source
topics.summary: Fill the preview from the open 5e SRD, with no account needed.
details: Enter an endpoint or slug such as /api/2024/classes/barbarian or /api/spells/acid-arrow. A list endpoint such as /api/2024/classes fetches every item it links to.
Pick a Template and Format, then select Generate Print to refresh with the latest data.

topics.title: Library Source
topics.summary: Print a record you've saved in Undercroft by picking its kind and name.
details: Kind lists the kinds of record in your Library. Item lists every saved record of that kind, or choose All to load every one as a list, one card each.
Records come from what you saved in Loom, or from generators such as Forge, which saves NPCs.

topics.title: JSON Upload Source
topics.summary: Load a JSON file from your device. It stays in your browser and is never uploaded.
details: Choose a .json file. Its contents are read locally for the preview and print.
After picking a Template, check that the file's fields match the Template's bindings, so the preview shows what you expect.
To refresh after changing the file, upload it again and select Generate Print.

topics.title: Manual Entry Source
topics.summary: Paste JSON that matches a Template, or leave it blank and work from Sample Data.
details: Paste JSON whose fields match the Template's bindings. The text is used in this page only; refreshing the page clears it.
Leave the box empty to preview and edit with the Template's Sample Data instead.

topics.title: Template, Format and Orientation
topics.summary: A Template decides which sizes and orientations are available; changing it refreshes both.
details: Format lists the paper or card sizes the chosen Template supports. Choose the one that matches your stock.
Orientation starts at the Template's recommendation. Some sizes allow only portrait or landscape.
Changing the Template resets Format and Orientation and rebuilds the preview.
Card Templates work out how many fit on a sheet from the cell size, gutters and margins for the Format you pick.

topics.title: Preparing to Print
topics.summary: A few settings that make cards and sheets come out aligned.
details: Print at 100% scale. Turn off “fit to page” or any shrinking in your print dialog, or card edges and margins won't line up.
For double-sided cards, print two-sided and flip on the long edge.
Print one test sheet before a bulk run, and check that the cut lines match on both sides.

topics.title: Template Properties
topics.summary: A Template's name, type, supported sizes and sources, and its card grid.
details: Choose New Template, Save, Duplicate Template or Delete Template in the toolbar. A Template's ID, Name and Description identify it in lists.
Type is Sheet, Card or Chip. Base font sets the default text font.
Formats are the sizes the Template supports, and Custom size lets you add one of your own by label, width and height in inches. Supported sources limits which Sources can use it.
Grid Properties set the cell width and height, gutter, safe inset, bleed, corner radius and number of columns and rows for card sheets.
Clear all uniqueness removes every per-card edit from the Template.

topics.title: Page Bindings
topics.summary: Set which part of the data each side uses and which lists repeat across the grid.
details: A data binding sets the starting point for a side, so every binding in it reads from a part of the data, such as one character or one spell, instead of the whole thing. Leave it empty to use all of it.
A repeat binding makes the card or chip grid repeat once for each item in a list, such as @features or @attacks.
Each side, front and back, has its own bindings.

topics.title: Palette and Layout
topics.summary: Build each side by dragging components from the Palette onto the preview.
details: Drag a component from the Palette onto the page. Double-click a Palette entry to add it to the end of the current side instead.
Drag components on the page to reorder them. Each side keeps its own layout, so use Show Back Side to build the back separately.
Select a component to edit it in the Inspector.

topics.title: Component Inspector
topics.summary: Select a component on the page to change its text, size, color, position and visibility.
details: Its sections follow the same order as the rest of the suite: Identity, the component's own settings, then Appearance, Behavior and Advanced, which start closed.
A List component treats each line of its text as a separate item, so bullet lists are quick to write.
Position and size can be set in inches or percentages. Image components also take a pan and zoom.
In Grid View, Make Unique applies a change to the one card on screen instead of the shared Template.
Changes show in the preview immediately and can be undone.

topics.title: Sample Data
topics.summary: The example JSON a Template previews with when no source data is loaded.
details: Edit it freely. It is saved in this browser as you type, and valid JSON updates the preview immediately. Invalid JSON is highlighted until you fix it.
Once source data is loaded, the panel shows that data instead.

topics.title: Saving and Loading Maps
topics.summary: Maps are saved records like everything else in the suite. Pick one from the Map list or start a new one.
details: Save lights up only after you've changed something since loading or saving.
Delete is enabled for maps you own, or have edit access to. Someone else's shared or public map stays view-only.
Signed out, your maps are saved in this browser only, like the other tools.

topics.title: Base Maps and Map Properties
topics.summary: A map starts from a base: an image you link to, or a tile map such as a real-world map.
details: For an image, paste its URL and set its width and height. For a tile map, enter a Tile Provider or choose a Quick pick such as Forgotten Realms, Eberron, Sharn: City of Towers or Real World.
Scale per cell and Scale unit tell the map how far one grid cell is, which measuring uses.
Initial Zoom and Initial Position set how the map first opens. Canvas Background sets the color behind the map.

topics.title: Layers and Groups
topics.summary: Everything you draw on a map lives on a layer, and groups collect cells and layers.
details: Add a layer from the Layers toolbar: Vector for drawn shapes, Grid for a square or hex grid with a cell size and line color, Raster for an image, or Marker for pins.
Select a layer to edit it in the Selection pane on the right.
A Group is a named set of grid cells, used for things like the revealed area of a fogged map. See Adding Grid Cells to a Group.

topics.title: Entity-Referencing Markers
topics.summary: A marker layer holds pins, and each pin can be linked to a saved record such as a Location, NPC or Monster.
details: Select a marker layer, then click empty space on the map to drop a pin. Click an existing pin to select and edit it, and drag a selected pin to move it.
In the pin's inspector, choose what kind of record it refers to and which one.

A pin linked to a record is outlined in the record owner's Player color, so changing that color recolors the pin everywhere. Turn off Use player color in the inspector to pick an outline for that pin yourself.
On a real-world map, pins are tied to actual coordinates, so they stay in the right place as you pan and zoom.

topics.title: Marker Contents
topics.summary: Any marker can hold items that a player claims by clicking it on the map: a chest, a crate, loot on a body.
details: Add a free-form item with a name and quantity, or choose Add Wonder to reference an existing Vault spell or magic item.
Claim Target decides where a claimed item goes: the clicking player's character inventory, or the group's shared Party Inventory.
A marker with unclaimed contents shows a small badge. A player who clicks it sees Claim buttons for what is left. Claiming takes just that one item, so several players can split a container.
Combine this with a marker's Hidden from Players switch to keep a container secret until you reveal it.

topics.title: Marker Resource Bar
topics.summary: Choose which Combat Binding resource the small bar above each combatant's marker shows.
details: This is a personal setting for this browser. It isn't saved into the System and doesn't affect anyone else.
It appears once your group has an active encounter in the Combat Tracker, and the bar always follows that encounter's live values.

Most Systems track only Hit Points, which is chosen automatically and marked “(auto-detected)”. This matters for a System with more than one resource, such as Action Points beside Hit Points, or Hope beside HP.

topics.title: Tiered Views
topics.summary: A View is a named preset that hides some layers from lower-tier viewers, such as a GM-only secrets layer.
details: The map's owner, or anyone with edit access, always sees every layer. Views only apply to someone viewing a shared or public map.
Each View lists the layers and groups it reveals and which account tiers see it. Leaving the tier list empty applies it to everyone.
A map with no Views shows every viewer every layer. Views are optional.

topics.title: Selecting Grid Cells
topics.summary: Add cells to a Group by clicking or sweeping across the grid, or edit several cells at once.
details: With a Group selected, click a cell, or click and drag across several, to add them to it straight away. This only adds cells; remove one with its Remove button in the Members list.
If the map has more than one grid layer and the Group isn't linked to a fog of war layer, “Paint on layer” appears so you can choose which layer your clicks affect.
You can also select cells first while a Layer is selected, then go to the Group and choose Add selected cells.
With more than one cell selected, the Custom Properties editor applies what you set to every selected cell. Select a single cell to see or change just that one.

topics.title: Fog of War
topics.summary: Hide every cell of a grid layer from other viewers, except the cells in its Reveal Group.
details: Turning it on creates an empty Group named “<layer name> — Revealed”, which is why nothing changes until you add cells. A Reveal Group with no cells means fog is on and nothing is revealed.
Add cells like any Group: select grid cells on the map, select that Group in the left pane's Groups list, and choose Add selected cells.
You never see the fog while editing, because the map's owner sees every cell. Check it from the Dashboard's Map widget as a player, or on a shared link.

topics.title: Auto-Reveal from Character Vision
topics.summary: Reveal fog around a character's marker automatically as it moves, using walls to block sight.
details: It works for a marker that is linked to a Character and has a Vision Range set on the marker itself. The range is never taken from the Character record automatically.
Vision Range can be a number, or bound to a field or formula on the linked Character, such as a Darkvision stat if that System has one.
Revealed cells, painted cells and placed Lights all combine into what is currently visible.

topics.title: Walls and Doors
topics.summary: Draw walls that block movement and sight, and doors you can lock or hide.
details: Click to add each corner of a wall, with a dashed line previewing the next piece. Double-click or press Enter to finish, Escape to cancel, and Backspace to remove the last corner.
Switch to Door in the type picker first to place a door. A door finishes as soon as you place its second point.
A wall's shape is set while you draw it. To change it, delete it and draw it again.
A Secret door looks exactly like a wall to anyone without full map access. A Locked door shows as a door but players can't open it. A door can be either, both or neither.
You always keep control with the Open/Close Door button in the inspector. Secret and Locked only limit what players can do by clicking a door on the Dashboard's Map widget.

topics.title: Dynamic Lights
topics.summary: A placed light glows and also reveals fog of war within its radius, stopped by walls, like a torch.
details: Range, Color and Opacity can all be changed after placing it, in the inspector.
A light never shines through a wall, whether or not Fog of War is on for the grid layer.
Attach a light to a token, in its inspector, to make it move with that marker, like a torch a character is carrying.

topics.title: Generating an NPC
topics.summary: Pick a Location, then Generate NPC to roll a full Identity and 4D set for it.
details: The Location determines the species weights and any archetypes it adds for itself. Everything else (Alignment, Gender, Attitude and the 4D tables) is the same everywhere.
Generate NPC rolls every attribute at once. After that, each Identity and 4D value has its own reroll button if you want to redo just one thing.
You can fix Species, Archetype, Alignment and Gender to a specific value instead of rolling them. See Fixing Specific Attributes.
The note is optional and separate. Add one afterward from the main pane; see Notes and Generate Note.

topics.title: Fixing Specific Attributes
topics.summary: Pick a Species, Archetype, Alignment or Gender to use that exact value, and leave any on “Random” to roll as usual.
details: Each choice starts on “Random”. Picking a value locks that one attribute for the next Generate NPC; everything else still rolls.
Species and Archetype options come from the selected Location. Alignment and Gender are the same everywhere.
These only affect the first Generate NPC roll. The reroll buttons on an NPC that has already been generated always roll fresh.

topics.title: Identity Attributes
topics.summary: Who this NPC is in the world, shaped by the selected Location.
details: Species, Archetype, Alignment, Gender, Age, Relationship and Attitude are concrete facts about this NPC.
Species and Archetype come from the selected Location and the System. Alignment, Gender, Age, Relationship and Attitude are the same everywhere.
Identity is what changes most from one Location to another. The 4D attributes never do.

topics.title: 4D Attributes
topics.summary: Personality and situation prompts for improvisation, the same for every Location and game system.
details: Description, Demeanor, Drive and Direction are one-word prompts. They are designed to stack, so rolling the same table twice can give you interesting tension rather than a contradiction.
They don't vary by Location or game system; they work for any NPC in any setting.
Treat them as a starting point for roleplay, not a fixed personality.

topics.title: Stats
topics.summary: The numbers for this NPC, either set by the Archetype or rolled independently.
details: A value the Archetype already defines, such as D&D 5e's ability scores, AC and HP, is looked up and updates whenever you generate or reroll the Archetype. A Location archetype can supply its own through its extra properties.

A value the Archetype doesn't carry, but that the System gives a minimum and maximum, is rolled independently instead of left blank. Call of Cthulhu's Characteristics, Hit Points and Move work this way.
A Location archetype with no extra properties has no fixed numbers. If the System also has nothing to roll independently, you see a note instead of numbers.

topics.title: Skills
topics.summary: For Systems that define skill generation, a few Key Expertise skills roll higher and the rest roll lower.
details: Which skills are Key Expertise is picked at random each time, not by occupation.
The skills, how many are Key, and both ranges come from the System, not from Forge. A different System can use entirely different numbers.
This section is hidden for a System with no skill generation set up.

topics.title: Features
topics.summary: Attach abilities from the shared Feature library to this NPC, picked by hand.
details: Pick a Feature from the list and choose Add. It appears below with its description.
A Feature with real mechanics, such as a weapon attack, a save effect or an active ability, opens a numbers editor when you click its row.
Remove takes a Feature off this NPC without deleting the shared Feature itself.
Unlike Monsters and Characters, nothing here is matched automatically, because Forge NPCs are generated rather than imported.

topics.title: Component Properties
topics.summary: Select a box in Identity to see its details in the right pane.
details: Selecting Species or Location opens the full editor for that Species Name Profile or Location.
Any other Identity box (Name, Archetype, Alignment, Gender, Age, Relationship, Attitude) shows the full table or profile behind that roll, beside this NPC's current value.
The pane is empty until you select something in Identity.

topics.title: Convert to Character
topics.summary: Turn a generated NPC into a Character you can open in Workbench.
details: In NPC Properties, choose Convert to Character, give the character a name and pick one of the Templates for the NPC's System.
The button is greyed out until the NPC has a System.

topics.title: Location Details
topics.summary: A Location's basics. Locations are created and edited in Sanctum.
details: Selecting a Location here only chooses which one to generate NPCs from. To create a Location or change its Type, Purpose, Environment, Features or Setting, open Sanctum.
Species Weights, Mixing Coefficient and Location Archetypes are the parts of a Location that Forge shows, since they're about how NPCs are generated there. Edit them in Sanctum.

topics.title: Species Weights
topics.summary: Each row picks a saved Species Name Profile and how common it is at this Location.
details: Forge draws from these rows to roll a new NPC's Species and Name.
Each row's list shows every Species Name Profile you've saved. Create one first if the species you want isn't there.
Weights are relative to each other, not percentages, so they don't need to add up to 100.
Together with the Mixing Coefficient, this population is why two Locations feel different even though the other tables are shared.

topics.title: Mixing Coefficient
topics.summary: One dial from 0 to 1 for how much a Location's species blend when naming an NPC: 0 is isolated, 1 is fully cosmopolitan.
details: At 0, names never blend: every NPC gets a plain name from its own species. As the number rises, blended names, shaped by two species at once, happen more often and go deeper.
It also decides who a name blends with. At low values the partner is always the Location's most common species. At high values it's a weighted random pick from everyone there.
And it decides how deep a blend goes: low values give a light borrow, one species' name with a short flourish from another. High values give a deeper blend.
At 1, blending always happens, the partner is always random, and the deepest blend is always used. It is never a hard on or off switch.

topics.title: Location Archetypes and Odds
topics.summary: A Location can add archetypes of its own, and the list's order sets how likely each one is.
details: The archetypes a Location can roll are its own, followed by the System's. A Location's archetype with the same name as a System one replaces it at that Location.

Each list is read most common first. Of N archetypes the first has the most weight, the next one less, down to the last, so adding or removing an archetype needs no re-weighting. For 20 archetypes the first comes up about 9.5% of the time and the last about 0.5%.
A Location's archetypes are listed first, so a local archetype is among the most common there. Reorder them, or add extra properties to give one its own stats, in Sanctum's Location Properties.
The Inspector lists every archetype the Location can roll, with its chance.

topics.title: Export Press Template
topics.summary: Save a printable NPC reference sheet for the selected Location as a Press template.
details: Select a Location and choose Export Press Template. A template named for the Location is saved to your account.
Open Press and pick that template to print the Location's NPC tables.

topics.title: Species Name Profiles
topics.summary: A species' example names, one per line, which Forge draws from when naming an NPC.
details: In Blended mode, First Names (and Last Names, if the species has them) are examples whose patterns Forge studies to make new names that sound like they belong, without handing back an exact line. A pool of 20 to 30 real names per list works well.
In Synonyms mode the lists are drawn from directly instead. See Name Mode.
Last Name Form (None, Family, Clan or Patronymic) only sets the label shown and whether a last name is generated at all. Use None for species with a single name.
A profile you save is reusable at every Location. Any Species Weights row can select it.

topics.title: Name Mode: Blended or Synonyms
topics.summary: Blended invents new names by recombining the sound patterns in your examples; Synonyms picks a name from the list as written.
details: Use Blended for species whose names are an invented language (Elf, Dwarf, Tiefling and most humanoids). The shared endings and syllables in the examples are what make new names sound right.
