Use Synonyms for species whose names are recognizable whole words in a theme, like a Changeling's Ashen, Doubt and Mirage, or a Warforged's Rivet, Piston and Bastion. Recombining letters across whole words gives nonsense, so the list is treated as a closed vocabulary.
A Synonyms species never takes part in name mixing, in either direction, whatever the Location's Mixing Coefficient is.
Name Mode belongs to the species, not the Location. A species is one or the other everywhere it's used.

topics.title: Generating a Monster
topics.summary: Choose a System, optionally fix some choices, then Generate Monster to build a stat block from shared Features.
details: A monster is made from a Creature Type, an Archetype and a Role, plus Features that fill the Archetype's recipe. Each choice you leave on “Random” is rolled.
Fix any of them, and the Combat Scaling level, before generating. See Fixing Specific Attributes.
After generating, you can edit the name and the numbers, and add notes. Save keeps it, and Convert to Character makes it a Character you can open in Workbench.
There is no reroll for one part. Generate again to try a new combination.

topics.title: Fixing Specific Attributes
topics.summary: Pick a Creature Type, Archetype or Role to use that exact value, and leave any on “Random” to roll as usual.
details: Each choice starts on “Random”. Picking a value locks that one for the next Generate Monster; everything else still resolves randomly.
Combat Scaling, Signature Feature and Locked Features work the same way: pin any of them to steer the result without building the whole monster by hand.
These only affect the next Generate Monster. To get a different combination, generate again.

topics.title: Combat Scaling
topics.summary: Pick the HP, AC and damage band a monster is built at, a rough equivalent of a challenge tier, or leave it on “Random”.
details: Each level sets a base HP, AC, damage per round, attack bonus, save DC and target Feature budget. Pinning a level fixes all of them together.
A Role's own tendencies multiply on top of the level, so two monsters at the same level can still come out quite different.
The levels are set up in Loom, so a System can define its own scale.

topics.title: Locked Features
topics.summary: Pin Features to guarantee they're included, instead of letting generation choose everything.
details: Locked Features are added first and count against the budget straight away, like the Signature Feature. Generation then fills the remaining slots around them.
They don't have to share a recipe slot or work together. Generation still tries to build a coherent monster around what you pinned.
Leave the list empty to let Crucible choose every Feature itself, guided by the Archetype's recipe and any Role or Creature Type you set.

topics.title: Identity
topics.summary: The Creature Type, Archetype and Role this monster ended up with, and its name.
details: Each is either what you fixed beforehand or a random pick from what's eligible.
The name is the only thing here you edit directly. Generate again to get a new set.

topics.title: Stats
topics.summary: Armor Class, HP, ability scores and Initiative Bonus worked out from the Combat Scaling level and Role. Edit them if you like.
details: HP and AC start from the level's base values and are adjusted by the Role, so a Brute and a Skirmisher at the same level differ.
Ability scores favor the ability the Role's damage relies on: Strength for melee-leaning roles, Dexterity for ranged-leaning ones, with Constitution scaled to the HP band.
Initiative Bonus is the Dexterity modifier. It's what the Combat Tracker's initiative roll uses once the monster is in an encounter.

topics.title: Features
topics.summary: The building blocks chosen for this monster: its Signature Feature plus the ones that fill the Archetype's recipe.
details: Each Feature was chosen because it works with what's already picked and doesn't conflict with it.
This list is exactly what is saved. There is no hidden layer of mechanics behind it.
A Feature with mechanics, such as an attack or save, opens its numbers when you select it.

topics.title: Recipe Fulfillment
topics.summary: Which of the Archetype's recipe slots were filled, and by which Feature.
details: A recipe is a signature slot plus required and optional slots. Each expects a Feature tagged for that slot and compatible with the Role and Creature Type.
An empty optional slot isn't an error. It just means nothing compatible was available, and the monster is still usable.

topics.title: Multiattack Attacks
topics.summary: List which of the monster's own Features it attacks with and how many times.
details: The Multiattack description writes itself from this list and stays in sync if you rename or edit one of those Features.
Use Add option for a real choice, such as “two Claws, two Bites, or one of each”. A single option shows no extra controls.
If a Multiattack is too irregular to describe this way, leave it as one empty option and the original text is shown exactly as typed.
Multiattack itself is one Feature shared by every monster. This list belongs to this monster only and saves when you save it.

topics.title: Editing a Feature
topics.summary: A Feature's name, description and cost can be changed in Loom, or here for a Unique one.
details: Fields for ID, Name, Description and Budget Cost can be changed here only for a Feature marked Unique in Loom, since it belongs to this one monster.
A shared Feature, such as Bite, Claw or Amphibious, is used by many monsters, so these fields are read-only. Choose Edit Feature to open it in Loom.

topics.title: Convert to Character
topics.summary: Turn a generated monster into a Character you can open in Workbench.
details: Choose Convert to Character, give the new character a name and pick one of the Templates for the monster's System.

topics.title: Generating a Wonder
topics.summary: Choose a System, optionally fix some choices, then Generate Wonder to build a spell or magic item from a budget.
details: A Wonder is a spell or magic item. Its Properties, such as Rarity, Activation and Item Form, set a budget, and Features are added until the budget is used.
If the System has casting classes, Casting Class narrows which Features are eligible. You can also fix any Property, choose a Signature Feature, or lock other Features before generating.
Once you open a saved Wonder, these generation choices are tucked away. They only matter when making something new.
Save keeps the Wonder. After generating, you can edit the name and the Features, and add notes.

topics.title: Locked Features
topics.summary: Pin Features to guarantee they're included, instead of letting generation choose everything.
details: Locked Features are added first and spend from the budget, or refund into it if their cost is negative, straight away, like the Signature Feature.
Generation then keeps adding the remaining Feature that works best with what's chosen and still fits the budget. A Feature with no synergy is never pulled in automatically.
Leave the list empty to let Vault choose everything, guided by the resolved Properties and Signature Feature.

topics.title: Identity
topics.summary: The Properties this Wonder ended up with, such as Rarity, Activation and Item Form, and its name.
details: Each Property is either what you fixed beforehand or a random pick from what's eligible.
The Property the System names as the budget ceiling sets the Feature budget's target. Every other Property's value spends from that budget, or refunds into it. That choice is made in Loom.
The name is the only thing here you edit directly. Generate again to get a new set of Properties.

topics.title: Features
topics.summary: The Signature Feature plus the Features added to use up the budget. Add or remove them to tweak the result.
details: Add a Feature from the list below at any time. Going over budget is allowed; the Remaining figure shows a warning instead of blocking you.
Features chosen by generation were checked for synergy and conflicts. A Feature you add by hand isn't checked, so it can create a conflict generation would have avoided.
Target, Spent and Remaining update live with every change, using the same budget math as generation.

topics.title: Editing a Feature
topics.summary: A Feature's name, description and cost are changed in Loom, not here.
details: These fields are read-only here. Every Feature is shared by many spells and items, so changing one from a single Wonder would change it everywhere it's used.
Choose Edit Feature to open it in Loom if it really needs changing.

topics.title: Generating a Location
topics.summary: Choose a System and Setting, optionally fix some choices, then Generate to build a Location.
details: A Location has a Type, a Purpose and an Environment, plus Features that give it character, and Assets and Needs.
Fix the Type, Purpose or Environment before generating, and lock any Features you want included. Everything left unfixed is rolled.
After generating, you can edit the name, adjust the Features, Assets and Needs, and add notes. Save keeps the Location.

topics.title: Setting
topics.summary: Choose which Setting a Location belongs to. Its name and description are edited under Setting Properties in the right pane.
details: A Setting belongs to one System (Forgotten Realms under D&D 5.5E, for example), and every Location belongs to one Setting (the Sword Coast under Forgotten Realms).
Leave this blank to start a new Setting with New Setting in Setting Properties, or pick an existing one to edit it or add Locations to it.

topics.title: Setting Species Weights
topics.summary: Optional. The Setting's general population, used by Forge for any Location here that has none of its own.
details: It has the same shape as a Location's own Species Weights: pick a Species and a relative weight for each one Forge should be able to roll.
A Location's own Species Weights always win when it has any. This list is used only when that Location's is empty, or when no Location is selected.
Leave it empty if every Location in this Setting will define its own population.

topics.title: Calendar
topics.summary: Optional. In-world calendar details for this Setting: months, weekdays, seasons and moon cycles.
details: Months is the only part a working calendar needs: an ordered list of names with a number of days each, such as Eberron's 13 months of 28 days. Uneven months work fine.
Days per week, Weekday Names, Seasons, Moon Cycles, Epoch label and Starting year are extras. Leave out any your Setting doesn't need.
Leave the whole section empty for a Setting that won't use a Calendar widget. A Dashboard Calendar widget can only use a Setting that has a calendar defined here.

topics.title: Location Properties
topics.summary: Optional settings Forge uses to generate NPCs at this Location. Not every place needs them.
details: Species Weights, Mixing Coefficient and Location Archetypes control Forge's species roll, name blending and archetypes for this Location.
A Location's own Species Weights come before the Setting's general ones. Leave them empty to fall back to the Setting's population.

Generic Name Fallback lists names to use when a rolled species is “Other” or can't be matched to a real Species. Each has a name and an optional weight, which is 1 if left blank; a higher weight is picked more often.
Leave the whole section empty for a Location that will never generate NPCs, such as a room or a building with no population.

topics.title: Location Archetypes
topics.summary: Optional. NPC types that only exist at this Location, rolled by Forge alongside the System's.
details: Add a row for each archetype and type its name. Drag the grip to reorder: the top of the list is the most common, and a Location's archetypes are rolled before the System's own.
Extra JSON is optional. Use the same keys the System's own archetypes use, for example {"armorClass": 12, "hitPoints": 11}. Without it, Forge rolls the System's usual ranges for that archetype.
Giving an archetype the same name as one of the System's replaces it at this Location, which is also a way to make a System archetype more common here by moving it to the top.
Leave the list empty if the Location needs no archetypes of its own.

topics.title: Identity
topics.summary: The Type, Purpose and Environment this Location ended up with, and its name.
details: Type and Purpose are either what you fixed beforehand or a random pick from what's eligible. Environment comes from the System's environment list, if it has one.
The name is the only thing here you edit directly. Generate again to get a new Type, Purpose and Environment.

topics.title: Features
topics.summary: The characteristics chosen for this Location, such as Fortified Walls, Black Market or Haunted.
details: Unlike Crucible and Vault there is no recipe or budget. One compatible Feature is chosen to start, then the best-fitting Feature that doesn't conflict is added until a randomly chosen count is reached.
A narrow, specific function, like “this place is a shop”, is a Feature rather than a Type or Purpose. Type and Purpose stay broad and Features add the specifics.
This list is exactly what is saved.

topics.title: Locked Features
topics.summary: Pin Features to guarantee they're included, instead of letting generation choose everything.
details: Locked Features start the selection, alongside or instead of the random starting Feature. Generation then keeps adding the compatible Feature that fits best.
A Feature with no synergy is never pulled in automatically, as in Crucible and Vault. Locking is how you force one in.
Leave the list empty to let Sanctum choose, guided by the Type, Purpose and Environment.

topics.title: Assets and Needs
topics.summary: What this Location has (Assets) and lacks (Needs). Usually Resources, but any saved record can be linked.
details: Generation fills these only with Resources: 1 to 3 Assets, then 1 to 3 Needs that don't repeat an Asset. To link a specific NPC, Monster or Wonder instead, use the kind and record pickers below each list.
Assets and Needs share one row shape (kind, linked record, label, description) and one way of adding rows, the same as Features.
They describe a place in broad strokes for a GM to use at the table. They aren't a simulated economy or ledger.

topics.title: Writing Pages
topics.summary: The Repository is a wiki-style journal for your game: pages of formatted text that link to each other and to your other records.
details: Pages are written in Markdown. Use View and Edit to switch between reading a page and changing it; the toolbar helps with headings, styles and inserting things.
Link to another page with its title in double square brackets, like [[Page Title]]. Refer to a saved record, such as an NPC or Location, with a name in backticks, like `npc:Name` or `location:Name`.

The left pane lists your pages in groups, with a search box above. The Outline, Tags, Parent, Related and Backlinks sections for the open page are in the same pane, and the last four open by themselves when the page has something to show.
Backlinks lists the pages that link to the one you're reading.

topics.title: Tags, Groups and Display Pills
topics.summary: Tags are plain text, but two prefixes, group: and display:, change how a page appears in the list.
details: A tag like group:Location puts the page under a “Location” group in the list. A / nests groups, as in group:Sessions/Arc 1.
A tag like display:Important shows “Important” as a small pill beside the page's title. A page can have several display: tags.
There is nothing else to set up: the tag's text is the whole instruction. Any other tag is an ordinary tag you can filter by.

topics.title: Parent Pages
topics.summary: Make one page the parent of another to nest it beneath that page in the list.
details: A page has one parent. Setting it nests the page under its parent in the list, however many levels deep.
This is different from a tag group or a Related link. It is a real parent and child relationship between two specific pages.

topics.title: Search Scope
topics.summary: Choose whether the page search also looks inside page text, not just titles and tags.
details: On (the default): search matches a page's title, tags and full text, so you can find a page by anything written in it.
Off: search covers titles and tags only. This is narrower, which helps once a common word turns up in dozens of unrelated pages.
A page that matches only in its text still appears in the list, and its group opens to show it while you search.

topics.title: Task Completion Dates
topics.summary: Choose whether checking off a task adds today's date to the end of its line.
details: On (the default): checking a task in View mode adds a date such as ✅ 2026-07-27 to the line.
Off: checking a task just marks it done.
Unchecking a task always removes its date.

topics.title: Quests
topics.summary: A [!quest] callout with a Markdown checklist inside it is a quest. There is no separate quest editor.
details: Write > [!quest] Quest Name, then a normal checklist below for the objectives. Its status (Not Started, Active or Complete) shows automatically from how many boxes are ticked.
Mention an NPC, location, monster or other record inside an objective the same way as anywhere else on the page: `npc:Name`, `location:Name`.

[[Quest Name]] links to a quest the way [[Page Title]] links to a page. A page title is tried first, so a quest link only works when no page has that exact title. [[Page Title#Quest Name]] is always unambiguous.
A quest belongs to the page it's written on, so its title only has to be unique on that page.

topics.title: Story Boards
topics.summary: A [!story-board] callout with a Nodes table and an Edges table is an interactive planning board.
details: Write > [!story-board] Board Name, then Layout: freeform or swimlane. For swimlane, add Lanes: and Stages: as comma-separated lists.

The Nodes table lists the cards. Each has a name, which is also how Edges refer to it, and optionally a Type (ref or placeholder), a Ref (such as kindId:Name or quest:Title) and a Lane, Stage, X, Y and Color.
The Edges table joins nodes by name: From, To and an optional Label.
A board belongs to the page it's written on, and a page can have several.
Switch between Freeform (drag cards anywhere) and Swimlane (a grid of lanes and stages) from the canvas toolbar at any time. Both layouts are stored on each card, so switching never loses anything.

topics.title: Date References
topics.summary: A `date:` code span shows as a formatted date chip against your group's calendar.
details: `date:123` shows Day 123 in the active Setting's calendar, or a plain “Day 123” if that Setting has none. Negative numbers count back from the group's Day 0.
`date:current` (or `date:today`) always shows the group's live date, wherever it appears.
Add a label with a pipe: `date:30|Festival begins` shows “Festival begins: ” and the date.
Every date reference also appears in the Timeline. A date chip is informational and doesn't mark anything overdue.

topics.title: Timeline
topics.summary: Every date reference across your pages, in order, grouped by day.
details: Each `date:` reference on any page is listed under its day, formatted with the active Setting's calendar.
A “Today” divider separates earlier entries from upcoming ones, using the same live date as the Calendar widget.
Click an entry to open the page it came from.
The list is built when you open the Timeline, and after you save a page, not continuously.

topics.title: Relationships Diagram
topics.summary: A diagram of how your pages, quests and referenced records connect, built from what you've already written.
details: Every [[Page Title]] link draws a connection between pages. A link that matches a quest connects to that quest.
Every record reference, such as `npc:` or `location:`, draws a connection from the page to that record.

The diagram is read-only and is built when you open it, and after you save a page, not continuously. It leaves out a Story Board's own planning layout, since that is a GM-only planning surface rather than game content.

topics.title: Running a Game
topics.summary: A step-by-step path from “I GM” to a live table.
details: Create a Group. This needs GM tier or higher; manage groups from the Groups tab in Loom.
Add your players' characters: open the group in Loom's Groups tab and pick characters for its roster.
Pick it as your Active Group with the group dropdown in the header, next to your account menu. It is there on every tool once you are signed in.
Share what the table needs: from any tool's Save/Export toolbar, or the Owned content list on your Account page, choose “Share with [your group]” for one click.
Show something live: add a Handout widget to your Dashboard (or a Map widget for maps) and click its eye icon. That is what the table sees.
Give players a way in: grab the group's public share link from Loom's Groups tab so players without accounts can read the Group Chat and Now Showing panel.

topics.title: Groups
topics.summary: A Group is how a GM organizes a table: an owner, a roster of characters, a threaded chat and a public share link.
details: Create one from Loom's Groups tab. This needs GM tier or higher.
Add players' characters to the roster from the same tab. The roster decides who can read and post in the group's chat while signed in.
Every group has a public share link, also in the Groups tab, so players without an account can read the chat and claim an unclaimed character.
Schedule real-world game sessions for the group from the Sessions section further down the same tab.

topics.title: Active Group
topics.summary: The group picker in the header sets the group every tool works with, and it follows you from tool to tool.
details: It lists every group you own or have a character in.
The active group is what one-click “Share with [active group]” buttons use, which group the Dashboard's widgets read from, and where your rolls are posted.
The choice is remembered in this browser, not on your account, so you need to pick it again on a different computer.

topics.title: Handouts and Now Showing
topics.summary: Put one card up in front of the table, live. Add a Handout widget to your Dashboard and click its visibility icon.
details: Add a Handout from the Dashboard's Edit layout toolbar. Pick the record (an NPC, Location, Monster or Wonder) and, if you like, a Press print template to draw it with. With no template, the table sees a plain name and description card.
Click the eye icon on the Handout's header to show it to your active group, and again to stop. The icon always reflects what is actually visible, even after a reload.
The record must already be saved. Showing an unsaved draft fails with a clear message instead of quietly showing nothing.
Maps work the same way from a Map widget, or from Orrery's signed-in menu. A map is always a plain link back into Orrery, never a card.
Anyone watching sees it in the Now Showing panel on the Dashboard and in Workbench, including players on the group's public share link. Showing something doesn't post anything in the chat.

topics.title: Group Chat
topics.summary: A threaded chat for the table: channels hold threads, and threads hold messages. It suits a live session and play-by-post alike.
details: Choose a channel and thread from the picker at the top. Every group starts with a General channel and thread, so a table that never adds more has one running log.
The newest messages sit at the top, with the box to write a new one above them.
Type @ to mention a person, a character or any saved record, and [[ to link a Repository page. Reply quotes the message you are answering. React with the emoji button; reactions never notify anyone.
You can edit or delete your own messages. The GM can edit or delete anyone's. A deleted message leaves a “message deleted” note so replies still make sense.

Rolls and other results, such as dice, card draws and shop and loot lines, are posted to the active thread, the one currently open in the chat. Dice and deck panels show which thread a roll will land in, and Private keeps a result to yourself.
Mentions, replies to your messages and direct messages arrive in your Inbox. Ordinary new posts show only as unread counts on threads and channels.
Anonymous visitors on a group's public share link can read the chat but not post.

topics.title: Channels and Threads
topics.summary: The GM organizes the chat into channels, and each channel into threads.
details: The GM creates channels, optionally under a category, linked to any saved record such as a Location, and set to in-character or out-of-character. A new channel asks for the name of its first thread.
The GM can let specific players start threads in a channel.
A thread's creator, or the GM, can archive it. See Archiving a Thread.

topics.title: Posting As
topics.summary: “Post as” chooses who is speaking: you, one of your characters, or for the GM, any NPC or Monster.
details: You can speak as yourself or as one of your own characters in this group, limited by the channel's mode. In an in-character channel you speak as a character; in an out-of-character channel, as yourself.
The GM can also speak as any NPC or Monster.
The last voice you used in a thread is remembered.

topics.title: Archiving a Thread
topics.summary: Archiving turns a thread's messages into a Repository page and makes the thread read-only.
details: The page is owned by the GM and shared with the group, and each message keeps its place so links to it still work.
Messages from an archived thread open its Repository page from your Inbox.
A thread's creator, or the GM, can archive it.

topics.title: Inbox and Direct Messages
topics.summary: Your Inbox collects what is aimed at you across every group: mentions, replies, direct messages and session invitations.
details: Open it from the account menu in any tool, or from the Inbox tab on your Account page. A badge shows how many are unread.
A mention is an @ of you or one of your characters. A reply is any message that quotes one of yours.

A direct message is a private note to one or more people in a group. It isn't posted in any thread and is never archived. Use the envelope button on a message to message its author. You can react to a direct message, and a reaction to a mention shows in the chat too.
Opening an item takes you to that message in the chat. Messages from an archived thread open its Repository page.
Session invitations, reminders and “not enough players” alerts arrive here too. See Session Invitations.
Delete removes an item from your Inbox. A session notice can be deleted only once that session has ended or been cancelled.

topics.title: Session Invitations
topics.summary: When your GM schedules a session, an invitation arrives in your Inbox for you to answer.
details: You're invited when you have an active character in the group. If you play more than one, choose which is active with “Playing as” on the invitation. You are then invited to upcoming sessions only.
The invitation always shows the session's current details and who has answered. Choose Accept, Tentative or Decline. Tentative answers are shown separately and don't count toward the minimum.
When a session is full, Accept becomes Join waitlist. If someone drops out before the session, the longest-waiting person is accepted automatically and gets a notice in their Inbox.
The GM can close RSVPs at a cutoff before the session. Your answer isn't counted until you give one.
Away for a while? Once you have declined a session, use “Decline a range” to decline every session between two dates in one go, including ones announced later.
You get a reminder before each session. You can delete a session notice once the session has ended or been cancelled.

topics.title: Account Tiers
topics.summary: Your tier decides which tools and kinds of record you can use.
details: From lowest to highest the tiers are Free, Player, GM, Creator and Admin. Each kind of record has its own minimum tier to read and to save. Most generator output is open to everyone; authoring-heavy kinds such as Systems need Creator or higher.
Signed out, you can use the tools in read-only mode and keep drafts in your own browser. Saving to the server needs an account.
Creating a Group needs GM tier or higher. Running a game is what GM tier is for, while Creator tier is about writing reusable content like Systems and Templates for others.
If someone sent you an invite link, creating your account through it can start you at a higher tier than Free.

topics.title: Upgrading Your Tier
topics.summary: Change your own tier from the Upgrade panel on your Account page. It's free for now, and billing arrives later.
details: Pick any tier up to Creator from the Upgrade panel on the right of your Account page. The change applies immediately.
No payment system is connected yet, so switching tiers, including down, is free and can be repeated as often as you like.
Admin can't be chosen here. Only an existing administrator can grant it.

topics.title: Account Settings
topics.summary: Change your email address and password, and set personal preferences.
details: Changing your email or password asks for your current password.

Player color is one color used in several places: your Dashboard background, and the outline of map tokens linked to your characters. You can set it here or in the Dashboard settings and the two always match. Until you pick one, the Dashboard uses the theme's own background and Clear takes you back to that.
Dice appearance sets how your 3D dice look, with a color for themes that allow one. Preview roll shows it.

topics.title: Owned Content
topics.summary: Everything you've saved, in one list, with sorting, filtering by type, and sharing.
details: Choose a Type to narrow the list, and click a column heading to sort by it.
The Share button on a row opens the sharing dialog for that record. The list shows only your own records; Loom's Library tab covers the whole library for those who manage it.

topics.title: Sharing Records
topics.summary: Give someone, or a whole group, access to a record you've saved.
details: A saved record can be shared with a specific person or with an entire Group. Sharing with a group gives every current member access and stays current as the group changes.
Each share is “view” or “edit”. View is the right choice for nearly anything shared with players.
Sharing works on anything you've saved: a Location, NPC, Monster, Wonder, Map, System, Template or Character. The record has to be saved first; sharing an unsaved draft fails with a message.

Share dialogs are in Loom's Library inspector, the Owned content list and the tools' own inspectors. Once you have an active group, they offer a one-click “Share with [active group]” beside the full picker.
A share link lets someone open a record without an account. Public sharing lets anyone view it.

topics.title: Finding a Game
topics.summary: Browse open listings, or people looking for a game or recruiting, and compare their preferences with yours.
details: Anyone can browse the open listings. Seeing a person's profile or history needs you to be signed in.
Filter listings by kind, system, platform, session length, age range, or a tag. The People view lists public profiles that say they are looking for a game or recruiting.
Each card shows how your own preferences compare: “Close on 3 of 5 shared scales”. You can sort listings by that. The comparison is never turned into a single score.
Pick a listing to see its schedule, its preferences side by side with yours, the GM's and members' history, and the Apply box.

topics.title: Your Profile
topics.summary: A profile tells GMs and players what you like and how you play. Everything on it is optional.
details: Open Account Settings and choose the Profile tab. A profile holds a bio, your role, experience, systems you know, other accounts, time zone, typical availability, preferred session length, safety tools, an open-to status and your preferences.

Other accounts lists your usernames on play services and social sites. Choose a service, type your username there and add it; each shows on your profile as a badge, linked to your page on that service where the service has one. Usernames aren't checked, so type them as they appear on the service.
Systems you type yourself, rather than pick from the list, are counted anonymously (a number only, never your name) to help decide which systems to add.
Profiles are private until you make yours public. A public profile also makes your history (see Signals) visible to other signed-in users.
“See how others see my profile” previews exactly what a visitor would see.
Choosing “Looking for a game” or “Recruiting” lists your public profile in the People view of Find a Game.

topics.title: Preference Scales
topics.summary: Thirteen five-point scales describe what you like in a game. Listings use the same scales, so they can be compared directly.
details: The first eight are the aesthetics of play: Presentation, Fantasy, Narrative, Challenge, Fellowship, Discovery, Expression and Relaxation.

The other five describe how a campaign feels, each between two poles: Tone (lighthearted to dark), Lethality (forgiving to deadly), Structure (sandbox to linear), Rules weight (rules-light to crunchy) and Seriousness (comedic to serious).
Every scale starts at “Don't care”. You can set one and later put it back. A scale set to “Don't care” is ignored when comparing.
“Close on N of M shared scales” counts the scales both sides have set that are within one point of each other. It is a quick read, not a rating.

topics.title: Location Privacy
topics.summary: Location is optional and you choose how precise it is. Only that precision ever leaves your browser.
details: Hidden shows nothing. Country shows only your country. Region shows your state, province or county.
Area is available in the United States only. You type your ZIP code, only the first three digits are kept, and it is shown as a place name such as “Chicago, IL”, never as digits.
Separately from location, you say whether you want in-person play, online play or both.

topics.title: Applying to a Game
topics.summary: Applying opens a private conversation with the GM, carried in both of your Inboxes.
details: Press Apply on a listing and write a short introduction. That message is the application. You can only have one pending application per listing.
The GM can Accept or Decline at any time while it is pending, and either of you can keep replying. Withdraw cancels your own application.
An application nobody answers is declined automatically after the period the GM set on the listing.

When you are accepted you join the group. From the application in your Inbox you can then claim a character from the GM's slate or add one of your own. Until you have an active character you receive no session invitations and cannot respond to sessions.

topics.title: Recruiting Players
topics.summary: A listing advertises one session or a whole campaign so players can apply.
details: Open the Groups tab in Loom, pick your group and use the Recruitment section. Your profile must be public first, because the listing shows your history.

A listing shows whether it is a session or a campaign, the system, the schedule (taken from the sessions themselves), open seats, the preference scales, tags, safety tools, session length, age range, platform, and the history of you and your current members.
You choose how many seats are offered and how many days an application can sit unanswered. The listing closes itself when every seat is taken and reopens if a seat frees up.
Applications arrive in your Inbox. Accepting adds the player to the group.

topics.title: Campaigns
topics.summary: A campaign is a named run of sessions inside a group.
details: Add campaigns in the Campaigns section of a group in Loom. A campaign is active, on hiatus or completed.
Every session belongs to its group and can also belong to a campaign, chosen when you create or edit the session. One-shots and session zeros need no campaign.
A completed campaign takes no new sessions. Deleting a campaign keeps its sessions; they just stop belonging to it.
Campaigns matter for retention and endorsements: leaving mid-campaign is counted, and you can endorse someone once for each campaign you played together.

topics.title: Players and Membership
topics.summary: A group's players are the people who belong to it, separately from their characters.
details: A player joins by being accepted from a listing, or when a character they own is added to the roster.

Removing a character from the roster does not remove the player. Use Remove player in the group's Players section to remove someone, which also takes their characters off the roster. A removal never counts against anyone.
Players can leave a group themselves from the Profile tab of Account Settings. Leaving while one of the group's campaigns is running counts as a departure.
A player with no active character in the group receives no session invitations and cannot respond to sessions.

topics.title: Signals, Not Judgments
topics.summary: Observed signals describe what has happened. They are not a verdict on anyone and are never combined into a score.
details: The signals are tenure, session count, sessions per system, reliability and retention. They are shown separately for games you have played and games you have run.
Each shows a recent window first, with lifetime figures beside it. Tenure is lifetime only.
Wherever a signal is a rate it shows its denominator, for example “6% · 18 sessions”. Below the minimum sample only the count is shown, because a rate from a handful of sessions says little.
There are no ratings and no written reviews. The only opinion on a profile is the endorsements people have chosen to give.

topics.title: Tenure
topics.summary: How long someone has had an Undercroft account.
details: Shown in whole years, or as “less than 1 year” for anyone newer.
Tenure is lifetime only and has no recent window. It says nothing about how often someone plays.

topics.title: Session Count
topics.summary: How many sessions someone has played or run, and with which systems.
details: As a player it counts the sessions you were Accepted for that took place, excluding any marked as a no-show. A contested no-show still counts, since it doesn't count against you.
As a GM it counts the sessions you ran: dates that were announced, not cancelled, and have ended.
Sessions per system groups the same counts by the system of the group they were played in.
There is no check-in. A session counts as having happened once its scheduled time has passed without being cancelled.

topics.title: Player Reliability
topics.summary: For players, reliability is the no-show rate.
details: A GM can mark a player who had Accepted a session as a no-show once it has ended. The player is told and can dispute it.
No-show rate = no-shows ÷ (sessions attended + no-shows), over sessions the player had Accepted. A disputed no-show is shown as contested and is left out of both numbers.

For play-by-post, a no-show is recorded automatically when a player accepted a posting window but posted nothing in the linked thread. It is only recorded when a thread is linked, and the GM can clear it.
A GM or an admin can clear a no-show, including a contested one.

topics.title: GM Reliability
topics.summary: For GMs, reliability is the cancellation rate, with late changes counted separately.
details: Cancellation rate = cancelled dates ÷ (dates run + dates cancelled), counting only dates that had been announced to players.
Ending a series is not a cancellation. Only cancelling an individual date is counted.
A cancellation or a change of start time is late when it comes after that date's cutoff for RSVPs. A date with no cutoff has nothing that can be late.
A cancellation because the players who had accepted fell below the minimum is counted as a cancellation but is never late.
Late cancellations and late reschedules are shown as counts beside the rate.

topics.title: Retention
topics.summary: Whether people stay through a campaign.
details: A participation is a player's first Accepted session in a campaign. A departure is a player leaving the group on their own while one of its campaigns is active or on hiatus. Someone who leaves before ever playing still counts as both.
Retention = 1 − departures ÷ participations. A departure counts against both the player who left and the GM.
Removal by the GM counts against nobody. Leaving after the campaign is completed counts against nobody.
A GM's retention pools every player across all their campaigns.

topics.title: Recent Window and Minimum Sample
topics.summary: Why some numbers show only a count.
details: The recent window is always the last 12 months; lifetime covers everything.
A rate is only shown once at least 5 cases are behind it. Below that, only the count is shown.

topics.title: Endorsements
topics.summary: A positive tag one person can give another after sharing a table.
details: Tags come from a list curated by an admin; each tag is for GMs, for players, or for both. There are no negative tags and no written reviews.

You can only endorse someone you have shared a table with, and only once per person for each campaign (or for each session that isn't part of a campaign). Neither of you can be a no-show for the date you shared.
Endorsements are shown as counts per tag. Who gave them is not shown to anyone.
Endorse people from the Profile tab of Account Settings, or from a session's notice in your Inbox once it has ended.

topics.title: Who Can See What
topics.summary: Public profiles are opt-in.
details: Your own profile and history are always visible to you, and to admins.
If you make your profile public, other signed-in users can see it and your history.
Without a public profile, your history is visible only to GMs of games you apply to and to people who share a group with you.
Anyone, signed in or not, can browse open listings, but profiles and histories need you to be signed in.

topics.title: Safety Tools
topics.summary: Techniques a table can use before, during and after play. Choose the ones you use.
details: Safety tools are grouped by when they are used. You pick any that apply on your profile, and a GM picks them on a listing.
Content topics themselves aren't tracked. They are meant to be settled at session zero, and a listing only signals them through its themes and safety tools.
Admins edit the list in Loom's Community tab.

topics.title: Listing Tags
topics.summary: Short tags that give the vibe of a game, like genre or mood, chosen from a curated list.
details: An admin curates the list in Loom's Community tab: add a tag, rename it, drag to reorder, or remove it. The list starts with a set of common genres.
When a GM adds a tag to a listing the curated tags are suggested, so similar listings use the same words. A GM can still type one that isn't on the list.
Renaming a tag, or renaming it to match another, updates every listing that carries it. Removing a tag takes it off every listing.

topics.title: External Services
topics.summary: The play services and social sites people can list their usernames on.
details: Admins curate the list in Loom's Community tab: add, change, remove or reorder services. Each has a name, whether it is a play service or social media, and an icon.
The icon is either an icon name such as tabler:brand-discord or the web address of an image, such as the service's favicon. A preview appears beside it.

A service can have a profile link, with {username} standing in for the person's username (for example https://github.com/{username}). Badges for that service then link to the person's page; leave it empty for services whose usernames don't map to a page.
Removing a service takes its badges off profiles. The usernames people typed aren't verified by the service.

topics.title: Chat Reactions
topics.summary: The emoji people can react with in group chat and the Inbox.
details: Admins curate the list in Loom's Community tab: add, change, remove or reorder emoji, and give each a short description shown as a tooltip when you hover over it.
A reaction never has a mechanical effect and never sends a notification.

topics.title: Fonts
topics.summary: The fonts Press and Workbench offer.
details: Creators add fonts from Press or Workbench. Admins can also edit, reorder and remove them from Loom's Community tab.
A font is a name and a CSS font-family. A Google Fonts name is optional and loads the font from Google when it's used.

topics.title: Audio Clips
topics.summary: The music and sound effects on the Dashboard's Soundboard.
details: GMs add clips from the Soundboard widget. Admins can also edit, reorder and remove them from Loom's Community tab.
A clip is a name and a link to an audio file, marked as music or a sound effect, and optionally set to loop.

topics.title: Map Tokens
topics.summary: The image links offered as map tokens and portraits.
details: GMs add tokens from the token picker. Admins can also edit, reorder and remove them from Loom's Community tab.
A token is a name and a link to an image hosted elsewhere.

topics.title: Page Sizes
topics.summary: The custom page sizes Press offers besides the standard ones.
details: Creators add custom sizes from Press. Admins can also edit, reorder and remove them from Loom's Community tab.
A size is a name with a width and height in inches.
